outcome: The conjecture itself remains open, but two papers since the frozen revision moved the best known asymptotic bound toward it: Montgomery & Sauermann (Aug 2025) proved (1-o(1))n disjoint transversal bases can always be packed (and (1+o(1))n suffice to cover), up from the prior (1/2-o(1))n; Arndt, Moseley, Pruhs, Swamy & Zlatin (Apr 2026) then gave the first polynomial-time constructive algorithm achieving an asymptotic version of this packing result for arbitrary matroids.
summary: Rota's basis conjecture (rank-n matroid with n disjoint bases can be arranged into an n×n matrix whose rows and columns are all bases) remains fully open as of September 2026. The most substantial development since the 26 January 2024 frozen revision is Montgomery & Sauermann, 'Asymptotically-tight packing and covering with transversal bases in Rota's basis conjecture' (arXiv:2508.05601, submitted 7 August 2025), which improves the best known asymptotic packing bound from (1/2-o(1))n disjoint transversal bases to the asymptotically-tight (1-o(1))n, and the covering bound from 2n (and later 2n-2) down to (1+o(1))n. I read the abstract and full text via fetch; it contains no reference to any AI or machine-learning system in its methods, acknowledgements, or elsewhere — this is a purely human, pen-and-paper (probabilistic/combinatorial) argument. A follow-up preprint, Arndt, Moseley, Pruhs, Swamy & Zlatin, 'Approximation Algorithms for Matroid-Intersection Coloring with Applications to Rota's Basis Conjecture' (arXiv:2604.03735, submitted 4 April 2026), constructivizes the Montgomery-Sauermann asymptotic packing result into the first polynomial-time algorithm achieving it, extending from representable matroids to arbitrary matroids; this is also purely human work with no AI mentioned. Both results are quantitative narrowings of the gap between the best proven packing/covering number and the full n the conjecture demands — they are bound-improving progress on the conjecture's own question (not a restriction to a special case, and not a different conjecture), so I classified the record as 'progress' rather than 'partial'. I also checked a 2024 result, Sauermann's 'Rota's basis conjecture holds for random bases of vector spaces,' but its arXiv submission (2203.17121) is dated 31 March 2022 with no later revision — only its European Journal of Combinatorics publication landed in 2024, which per the dating rule (first public written argument, not journal date) puts the actual event before the frozen revision date, so it is excluded (not counted, not even open_stale, since the actual submission genuinely predates the article's freeze and is irrelevant to what changed in the window). I also found a 2024 paper on the 'Latin Tableau Conjecture' (Chow & Tiefenbruck, arXiv:2408.04086), a generalization (wide partition conjecture, in the free-matroid case) of Rota's basis conjecture with computational verification of low-order cases; this changes a different, more general question rather than the stated bullet, so under §3.1 it is a related problem, not a case, and I did not let it affect the status here. No source anywhere — triage's own found item, the Wikipedia article, EmergentMind, Open Problem Garden, or my own searches — surfaced any AI system near this problem in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the Montgomery-Sauermann and Arndt-et-al results are significant enough progress on a 30-year-old conjecture to warrant more prominence than 'progress' conveys, but per §6.1 'progress' is exactly the code for a bound that moved while the problem stays open, which is precisely what happened; there is no case of the conjecture (e.g., a specific matroid class or fixed small n) that was newly settled, so 'partial' would overstate what occurred.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) removing the o(1) term entirely — i.e., establishing exactly n disjoint transversal bases (or a counterexample) for arbitrary matroids — would resolve the conjecture itself; short of that, any paper explicitly crediting an AI system with producing part of the combinatorial argument in a future preprint would change the ai_role.
